rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Triliteral nouns followed by the two feminine alifs retain the post-diminutive consonant and both alifs, as in ḥumayrāʾ and ṭurayfāʾ.
rows.anchor: لا تكسر الحرف الذي بعد ياء التصغير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿlān nouns with a feminine faʿlā counterpart keep the nūn in diminutive because it follows an alif and substitutes for the feminine alif, like the hamza in ḥamrāʾ.
rows.anchor: ألف وكانت بدلا من ألف التأنيث حين أرادوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A five-letter noun ending in nūn after alif, matching faʿlān but not broken on mafāʿīl, takes the same diminutive pattern as faʿlān/faʿlā.
rows.anchor: حروف فعلان الذي له فعلى توالت فيه ثلاث حركات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A declinable triliteral noun with two added letters and a long hamza diminutivizes like a same-length noun whose hamza replaces a root yāʾ, as ʿalbay and ḥurayb.
rows.anchor: فكان ممدودا منصرفا فإن تحقيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Where the replaced root yāʾ is visible, the diminutive keeps it, as in daraḥiya → durayḥiya, because the added letters are not feminine markers.
rows.anchor: حقرت ذلك الاسم كما تحقر الاسم الذي ظهرت فيه ياء

rows.speaker: من قال غوغاء
rows.claim: Those treating ghawghāʾ as masculine and declinable like qaḍqāḍ form its diminutive ghwayghī.
rows.anchor: من قال غوغاء فجعلها بمنزلة

rows.speaker: من لم يصرف وأنث
rows.claim: Those treating ghawghāʾ as feminine and indeclinable form ghwayghāʾ, on the pattern of ʿuwayrāʾ.
rows.anchor: ومن لم يصرف وأنث فإنها عنده بمنزلة عوراء

rows.speaker: من قال قوباء
rows.claim: A speaker who declines masculine qūbāʾ forms quwaybī, like ʿalbay.
rows.anchor: ومن قال قوباء فصرف قال قويبي كما تقول عليبي

rows.speaker: من قال هذه قوباء
rows.claim: A speaker treating qūbāʾ as feminine and indeclinable forms quwaybāʾ, like ḥumayrāʾ, because it has the feminine alifs on a triliteral base.
rows.anchor: فأنث ولم يصرف قال قويباء كما قال حميراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A faʿlān noun broken on mafāʿīl takes a diminutive like sirbāl because its broken plural governs the treatment; examples include sarḥān, ḍabʿān, ḥawmān, sulṭān, and farzān.
rows.anchor: شبهوه به حيث كسر للجمع كما يكسر سربال

rows.speaker: من قال فرازنة
rows.claim: Those pluralizing farzān as farāzina still use furayziyyīn in diminutive, since it has a broken plural like jaḥājiḥa and zanādiqa.
rows.anchor: فريزيين لأنه قد كسر كما كسر جحجاح وزنديق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ẓarbān becomes ẓuraybān because its plural ẓarābī drops the nūn, unlike sirbāl’s retained root lām; treat its plural as ẓarbāʾ.
rows.anchor: كأنك كسرته على ظرباء ولم تكسره على ظربان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Warshān is diminished as warayshiyyīn because its plural is warāshīn.
rows.anchor: وتقول في ورشان وريشيين لأنك تقول وراشين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If a sarḥān-like noun has no known broken plural, use the faʿlān/faʿlā diminutive by analogy until its plural is known.
rows.anchor: إذا جاء شيء على عدة حروف سرحان وآخره كآخر سرحان

rows.speaker: يونس وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: Yūnus and Abū ʿAmr give sarḥān → surayḥīn; proper-name diminutives retain this pattern.
rows.anchor: ولو سميت رجلا بسرحان فحقرته لقلت سريحين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Proper names such as ʿalqā and maʿzā take ʿulayqī and muʿayzī, while a woman named sirbāl takes suraybāl; diminutive formation stays regular even when the name is indeclinable.
rows.anchor: ولو قلت سريحان لقلت في رجل يسمى علقى عليقي

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Sībawayh attributes the material in this chapter and the next to Yūnus.
rows.anchor: الباب الذي يليه قول يونس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common pausal form drops final yāʾ in nouns such as qāḍ, ghāz, and ʿamī, as it drops before tanwīn in connected speech.
rows.anchor: هذا قاض وهذا غاز وهذا عم تريد العمي

rows.speaker: أبو الخطاب ويونس
rows.claim: Abū al-Khaṭṭāb and Yūnus report trusted Arabic speakers who retain final yāʾ at pause when there is no tanwīn; clear pronunciation is better in that setting.
rows.anchor: وحدثنا أبو الخطاب ويونس أن بعض

rows.speaker: بعض العرب
rows.claim: Some Arabs also delete yāʾ at pause in definite forms, by analogy with indefinite nouns where yāʾ drops before tanwīn; yāʾ plus kasra is heavy.
rows.anchor: ومن العرب من يحذف هذا في الوقف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the accusative yāʾ must be clear because it remains in connected speech and, once moving, behaves like a sound noun.
rows.anchor: وأما في حال النصب فليس إلا البيان

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl prefers vocative yā qāḍī, paralleling al-qāḍī, because the vocative is not nunated.
rows.anchor: فقال أختار يا قاضي لأنه ليس بمنون

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus prefers yā qāḍ; Sībawayh calls this stronger because deletion occurs outside vocatives and vocatives readily omit material, as in yā ḥār and yā ṣāḥ.
rows.anchor: يا قاض وقول يونس أقوى لأنه لما كان من كلامهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At pause, marrī compensates for retaining the form rather than dropping both hamza and yāʾ together.
rows.anchor: وقالا في مر إذا وقفا هذا مري كرهوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verbs do not normally lose final yāʾ at pause because it remains in connected speech; lā adri is an exceptional frequent form, compared with lam yak, and deletion is restricted to lā adri and mā adri.
rows.anchor: وأما الأفعال فلا يحذف منها شيء لأنها لا تذهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Final weak letters may be deleted in Qurʾanic cadence and rhyme even where speech normally retains them; Sībawayh cites four Qurʾanic endings.
rows.anchor: وجميع ما لا يحذف في الكلام وما يختار فيه أن لا يحذف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nouns are especially liable to deletion because they also show it outside cadence and rhyme.
rows.anchor: والأسماء أجدر أن تحذف إذ كان الحذف فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although retaining yāʾs and wāws is more analogical, deletion is also common Arabic; Zuhayr’s verse illustrates retention in cadence.
rows.anchor: وأراك تفري ما خلقت وبعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some Arabs vocalize the consonant before a final consonant in pause to avoid two adjacent quiescent consonants; Sībawayh illustrates with bikr.
rows.anchor: وذلك قول بعض العرب هذا بكر ومن بكر

rows.speaker: الراجز من بني سعد
rows.claim: A Saʿdī rajaz poet uses al-naqri intending al-naqru, a pausal form; ordinary speech uses al-naqru in nominative and other cases.
rows.anchor: أنا ابن ماوية إذ جد النقر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ʿudl and fisl, speakers harmonize the following vowel with the preceding kasra, unlike the earlier pattern because faʿl is not usual here.
rows.anchor: ما فعلوا بالأول لأنه ليس من كلامهم فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With al-busr, they carry the first vowel forward rather than use the unattested faʿl pattern; these speakers lighten it in connected speech.
rows.anchor: وقالوا في البسر ولم يكسروا في الجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In al-ʿukm they do not open the kāf in the accusative; the preceding ḍamma is treated as if it followed, as in al-ḥajr.
rows.anchor: وهو قولك رأيت الجحر وإنما فعلوا ذلك في هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This vowel treatment does not occur with Zayd or ʿawn because yāʾ and wāw are long vowels that tolerate it; applying it to alif would change the letter.
rows.anchor: ولا يكون هذا في زيد وعون ونحوهما لأنهما حرفا مد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qāf, jīm, ṭāʾ, dāl, and bāʾ are qalqala stop letters: at pause they release an audible sound because of articulatory pressure.
rows.anchor: وذلك القاف والجيم والطاء والدال والباء

rows.speaker: بعض العرب
rows.claim: Some speakers produce the qalqala sound more strongly, as if they were trying to pronounce a vowel.
rows.anchor: وبعض العرب أشد صوتا كأنهم الذين يرومون الحركة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zāy, ẓāʾ, dhāl, and ḍād release a softer, breath-like sound at pause as air escapes; ḍād vents between the molars.
rows.anchor: خرج معها نحو النفخة ولم تضغط ضغط الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All voiceless letters have audible breath at pause because they are produced with exhalation rather than chest voice; some speakers make it stronger.
rows.anchor: وأما الحروف المهموسة فكلها تقف عندها مع نفخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lām, nūn, mīm, ʿayn, ghayn, and hamza have no comparable release at pause because their articulations lack pressure or an opening.
rows.anchor: لا تسمع بعدها في الوقف شيئا مما ذكرنا لأنها لم تضغط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These pause sounds do not occur in connected speech because the next sound begins before articulatory release develops.
rows.anchor: لا يكونان فيهن في الوصل إذا سكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh demonstrates connected forms such as ayqiẓ ʿumayran and aḥriz mālan, and directs the reader to hear breath in pausal afrish, aḥbis, faẓẓ, and khudh.
rows.anchor: وذلك قولك أيقظ عميرا وأخرج حاتما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamza following a quiescent consonant has several pausal realizations, including forms with a hinted or applied case vowel.
rows.anchor: أما كل همزة قبلها حرف ساكن فإنه يلزمها في الرفع والجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many Arabs, especially Tamīm and Asad, vocalize the consonant before hamza to clarify hamza, which is especially faint at pause.
rows.anchor: حركوا ما قبلها ليكون أبين لها وذلك قولهم

rows.speaker: ناس من بني تميم
rows.claim: Some Banū Tamīm say al-radiʾ rather than add ḍamma after kasra, rejecting a faʿl sequence, and regularize accusative and al-baṭʾ similarly.
rows.anchor: لأنه ليس في الكلام فعل فتنكبوا هذا اللفظ

rows.speaker: من العرب
rows.claim: Some speakers replace final hamza with wāw in the nominative, yāʾ in the genitive, and alif in the accusative while keeping the preceding consonant quiescent.
rows.anchor: حرصا على البيان ويقول من الوثى فيجعلها ياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Speakers who avoid the preceding-vowel strategy should consistently retain the corresponding wāw or yāʾ alternatives.
rows.anchor: فإنه ينبغي لمن اتقى ما اتقوا أن يلزم الواو والياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the consonant before hamza already has a vowel, hamza takes the usual pausal options; the same applies when a quiescent preceding consonant is first moved.
rows.anchor: وذلك قولك هو الخطأ وهو الخطأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Speakers avoid doubling final hamza, so it otherwise behaves like a nonweak consonant except in replacement and gemination.
rows.anchor: الهمزة بمنزلة ما ذكرنا من غير المعتل إلا في القلب والتضعيف

rows.speaker: من العرب
rows.claim: Some speakers replace final hamza in al-kalʾ with wāw, yāʾ, or alif according to case, as in the variants of al-wathʾ.
rows.anchor: ومن العرب من يقول هذا هو الكلو حرصا على البيان

rows.speaker: أهل الحجاز
rows.claim: Hijazi speakers who do not realize hamza pronounce a quiescent hamza after fatḥa as alif in every case; no ishām applies because it is like the dual alif.
rows.anchor: فأما الذين لا يحققون الهمزة من أهل الحجاز فقولهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For softened hamza after ḍamma or kasra, the replacement is wāw or yāʾ respectively, without ishām, as in akmū and ahnā.
rows.anchor: ولو كان ما قبلها مضموما لزمها الواو نحو أكمو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When hamza after a quiescent consonant is softened, it must be deleted; the consonant that receives its movement then follows ordinary pausal rules for nonweak consonants.
rows.anchor: ورأيت الوث والخب ورأيت الخب وهو الخب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Across word boundaries, assimilation of identical moving consonants is best when it yields five or more consecutive moving segments; such sequences are generally avoided in five-letter words.
rows.anchor: فأحسن ما يكون الإدغام في الحرفين المتحركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetic meter supports the preference: five moving consonants do not occur consecutively in verse, though clear pronunciation remains good Hijazi Arabic.
rows.anchor: خمسة أحرف متحركة وذلك نحو قولك جعل لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike assimilation within a word, separate words can be pronounced distinctly because the second word need not begin with the matching consonant.
rows.anchor: ولم يكن هذا بمنزلة قد واحمر ونحو ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilation is also good when another moving matching consonant precedes the pair and a quiescent consonant follows, as in yad Dāwūd.
rows.anchor: حسن الإدغام وذلك نحو قولك يدداود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The more consecutive movements there are, the better assimilation becomes, though distinct pronunciation remains permissible.
rows.anchor: وكلما توالت الحركات أكثر كان الإدغام أحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A long vowel before matching moving consonants counts like a moving segment, so assimilation is good in examples such as inna al-māla laka.
rows.anchor: فإن الإدغام حسن لأن حرف المد بمنزلة متحرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A long vowel acts like a moving segment and supplies the raddif required when a moving segment is deleted in rhyme; the yāʾ in the cited poetry supplies the raddif.
rows.anchor: حرف المد بمنزلة متحرك أنهم إذا حذفوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If a quiescent consonant precedes the first matching moving consonant, it cannot be silenced; speakers may hide it with moving weight because boundary assimilation does not change word structure.
rows.anchor: حرف ساكن لم يجز أن يسكن ولكنك إن شئت أخفيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Examples such as ibn Nūḥ and ism Mūsā retain their forms; assimilation shifting a consonant inside one word can delete its alif, as in رد and قل, while cross-word assimilation would alter the word's structure.
rows.anchor: لا تدغم هذا فلو أنهم كانوا يحركون لحذفوا الألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Silencing is not allowed in qurādd or lahāmm because it would impose a plural pattern unlike their singulars; poems by an unnamed poet and Ghaylān b. Ḥurayth support concealment.
rows.anchor: لأن قرددا فعلل ولهمما فعلل ولا يدغم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A reading with kasra in ʿayn of niʿimmā follows the dialect that vocalizes ʿayn; Abū al-Khaṭṭāb identifies it as Hudhayl, and Ṭarafa’s verse supports the form.
rows.anchor: وحدثنا أبو الخطاب أنها لغة هذيل

rows.speaker: أهل مكة
rows.claim: For falā tatanājaw, the first tāʾ may be quiescent after the long vowel or concealed with moving weight; Meccans reportedly do not fully articulate both tāʾs.
rows.anchor: وزعموا أن أهل مكة لا يبينون التاءين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In thawb Bakr, clear articulation is better than after a long vowel because the preceding vowel is not part of the same word; concealment or silence remains possible with long-vowel letters.
rows.anchor: لأن حركة ما قبله ليس منه فيكون بمنزلة الألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The yāʾ in diminutive ṣuwaym is not moved, resembling alif in plural patterns; this permits concealment or, with its length, silence.
rows.anchor: قولهم أصيم فياء التحقير لا تحرك لأنها نظيرة الألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A final long wāw or yāʾ followed by the same initial sound in the next word is not assimilated, as in dalw Wāqid and ẓaby Yāsir.
rows.anchor: وتقول هذا دلو واقد وظبي ياسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With final long yāʾ or wāw followed by the same sound, speakers may conceal or articulate across the boundary but cannot silence it because that removes length; rhyme evidence confirms this.
rows.anchor: ولا تسكن لأنك حيث أدغمت الواو في عدو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A wāw after ḍamma or yāʾ after kasra is not assimilated across a word boundary; speakers preserve the long vowel and the form's weight.
rows.anchor: إذا كانت الواو قبلها ضمة والياء قبلها كسرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In imperatives such as ikhshi Yāsiran and ikhshū Wāqidan, assimilation occurs because these yāʾs and wāws are not long vowels in this use.
rows.anchor: لأنهما ليسا بحرفي مد كالألف وإنما هما بمنزلة قولك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two hamzas are not assimilated because speakers must preserve distinct pronunciation; Ibn Abī Isḥāq and his associates used assimilation, which Sībawayh calls poor but permissible for them.
rows.anchor: لأنك لا يجوز لك أن تقول قرأ أبوك فتحققهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In iftaʿala forms such as iqtatalū and yaqtatilūn, speakers may show or conceal the matching tāʾs; unlike fixed gemination in iḥmarra, the infix tāʾ need not be followed by its matching radical.
rows.anchor: إن شئت أظهرت وبينت وإن شئت أخفيت وكانت الزنة

rows.speaker: بعض العرب
rows.claim: Some Arabs fully assimilate the tāʾs in a single word, quiescing the first; others transfer its movement to the prior consonant, with both forms possible in these flexible sequences.
rows.anchor: فأسكن لما كان الحرفان في كلمة واحدة ولم يكونا منفصلين

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan’s reading illā man khaṭifa al-khaṭfata supports the account of assimilation and alternative vocalizations of the preceding consonant.
rows.anchor: وتصديق ذلك قول الحسن إلا من خطف الخطفة

rows.speaker: الخليل وهارون
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl and Hārūn report speakers saying murdifīn for murta difīn; this is a Meccan reading, with muqtalīn a rarer parallel and radif for irtadaf in another dialect.
rows.anchor: وحدثني الخليل وهرون أن ناسا يقولون مردفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alif in ألْحمر is retained after moving lām because it resembles hamzat qaṭʿ: it opens initially and remains under interrogation; similar strengthening occurs in other phrases.
rows.anchor: فلأن هذه الألف قد ضارعت الألف المقطوعة نحو أحمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilation in iqtatalū is as good as across-word jaʿal laka, though adjacency also makes it resemble the fixed gemination of iḥmarra.
rows.anchor: إلا أنه ضارع حيث كان الحرفان غير منفصلين احمررت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no concealment in اردد because the consonant is between two quiescent letters; رد داود behaves like اسم موسى, with assimilation only when the preceding segment is moving.
rows.anchor: فكذلك ضعف هذا إذ كان بين ساكنين
